old_title: Markets drop ahead of Nvidia's results; China pledges 'necessary measures' against US AI chip restrictions - business live
new_title: Markets drop ahead of Nvidia's results; Jensen Huang says he'd be 'honoured' to return as CEO - as it happened
old_text:
Stock markets on both sides of the Atlantic are dropping deeper into the red.
The DowJonesIndustrialAverage is now down 1%, having lost 511 points to around 51,096 points.
And in London, the FTSE100 index is down 1.4%, having dropped by 154 points to 10,726 points.
Investors may be getting jittery ahead of Nvidia's results tonight, to be followed by Anthropic's IPO on Thursday.
Reminder: Wall Street will hear from Nvidia's interim CEO, ColetteKress, tonight, following the resignation of JensenHuang last week after allegations that he conducted an affair with a suspected Chinese spy.
Nvidia will also face questions about claims that billions of dollars of its chips were sold to China, and about the implications of the US closing a loophole that allowed Chinese companies to access Nvidia-powered data centres in other countries.
Joe Mazzola, head trading & derivatives strategist at CharlesSchwab, says:
The chip giant typically releases results about half an hour after the close. Nvidia's call follows at 5 p.m. ET, led by CFO and interim CEO Colette Kress. If a board member or executive besides Kress speaks prominently, speculation might rise about where they stand in the Huang succession stakes. Investors could hear plenty of scuttlebutt on the CEO topic after the call.
The biggest question is whether Nvidia can keep growing parabolically without Huang at the helm. Outlook is paramount, and a devastating outcome would be if Nvidia pulls guidance. Back in August, Nvidia forecast fiscal 2028 revenue growth of 70%. See if the company sticks to that. Export controls on advanced chips are another topic, especially after the U.S. took new measures to limit remote access to advanced AI chips.
Shares fell more than 4% Monday as investors prepared for worst-case scenarios, and big share moves are priced in for Nvidia depending on the outcome. If the call gets an optimistic take, the entire sector could feel relief. Though quarterly results might seem secondary, earnings are seen up 90.4% to $2.48 per share and revenue is seen up 91.3% to $109.1 billion.

Jensen Huang and Nvidia agree to appear before Congress
Ousted Nvidia CEO JensenHuang, and the chipmaker's general council TimTeter, have both agreed to testify to three congressional committees next month.
Huang and Teter have voluntarily agreed to appear before the House Foreign Affairs Committee, the Select Committee on the Chinese Communist Party, and the House Intelligence Committee for transcribed interviews, the chairs of the three committees say.
House Foreign Affairs Committee Chairman BrianMast, Select Committee on China Chairman JohnMoolenaar, and House Permanent Select Committee on Intelligence Chairman RickCrawford had invited the two men to testify last week.
Chairmen Mast, Moolenaar, and Crawford said in a statement, just released:
"We look forward to hearing from Jensen Huang and Tim Teter on their roles in a potential breach of our national security.
"The American people need answers on Mr. Huang and Nvidia's role in allowing dangerous PRC actors to access our most advanced chips, as well as the role of a potential Chinese intelligence asset in this scandal."
Huang will appear before the committees on December 1st, and Teter will appear on December 2nd.
New data from AlphaSense has found that mentions of Nvidia on global corporate earnings calls have surged 48% over the first nine months of this year, compared to the same period in 2025.
This highlights Nvidia's "growing influence across the wider business ecosystem", they say.
US stocks have opened gingerly, ahead of Nvidia's results at the end of the trading day.
The benchmark S&P 500 share index dropped by 0.28% at the start of trading.
The DowJonesindustrialaverage, which contains 30 large US companies, has dropped by 404 points or 0.8% to 51,203 points. UnitedHealth (-4.5%) are the top faller.
The tech-focused Nasdaq index dipped by 0.09%, with Nvidia's stock flat in early trading too...
Here's a great chart from JimReid at DeutscheBank, showing how Nvidia's earnings have soared since the AI boom began, and how they are expected to keep accelerating:
He explains:
Forget the macro, the biggest event of the next few weeks is probably tonight's Nvidia earnings. It's a good moment to remember that the company's transformation is arguably one of the most extraordinary in corporate history.
When ChatGPT launched in November 2022, Nvidia was earning around $5bn a year. That was a respectable number for a company still best known to gamers and crypto miners. Today, on a rolling four-quarter basis, it's likely to be nearer $240bn, and consensus has it reaching around $625bn by 2031. If that happens, Nvidia will have gone from $5bn of net income to over $600bn in under a decade.
I can't think of anything that comes close. The biggest annual profit ever reported is generally thought to be Saudi Aramco's roughly $160bn in 2022, when oil was last above $100 and Europe was scrambling for energy. Nvidia is now ahead of this. Its 2031 forecast would be about the size of the current annual GDP of Thailand, the UAE or Austria. Those countries have populations of around 72m, 11.5m and 9.2m respectively.
Nvidia, at its last filing, employed around 42,000 people. Yes, it's apples and oranges, or perhaps chips, but it shows the sheer scale of what's going on.
Responding to the European Commission's charge sheet announced earlier (12.08) a Temu spokesperson said they "respectfully disagreed" with the findings.
The spokesperson said:
Temu invests significantly in compliance infrastructure and human expertise and implements a suite of control measures that effectively mitigate illegal product risks with a consistently low incidence of problematic products.
Promising to respond to the findings carefully, the company added:
We are confident that we will reach an amicable resolution of the matter that fully addresses the Commission's remaining concerns.
US government confirms investigation into Megaspeed over Nvidia chip exports
Two US government departments have confirmed they are investigating computing company Megaspeed, suspecting it of violating US export controls by helping to ship tech giant Nvidia's chips to China.
A joint statement issued by the Department of Commerce and the Department of Justice explains that Megaspeed has been under investigation since 2024, for "potential export control violations."
In May 2025, Department of Commerce investigators requested records from Nvidia concerning direct or indirect sales to Megaspeed. In June 2025, Nvidia placed Megaspeed on its "no sell" list, they explain.
And they also state that commerce department agents conducted an on-site, in-person, end-use check at Megaspeed in June 2025 and interviewed CEO Alice Huang.
The Department of Justice then took the lead role in the criminal investigation of Megaspeed.
Tooting their own trumpets, the departments add:
This investigation is the result of the excellent work of the Department of Commerce under Secretary Howard Lutnick and the law enforcement efforts of the Department of Justice under Attorney General Todd Blanche.
That, presumably, is a response to suggestions that Lutnick could be fired following accusations that he had shielded Nvidia from federal oversight, and had failed to blacklist Megaspeed.
new_text:
Jensen Huang has thrown his hat into the ring to return to his role running Nvidia, less than a week after being ousted amid an alleged spy scandal.
Huang has issued a statement admitting making "serious mistakes" in his personal life - a nod to his previous admission of cheating on his wife, allegedly with a suspected Chinese spy.
He says:
I created problems for the Board that I deeply regret. I own my mistakes completely, and I am committed to cooperating with the Board's independent investigation.
But Huang also indicated he would be happy to return to his role, saying:
Since my departure, I've seen an outpouring of calls from Nvidia's employees, investors, business partners, and customers for me to return as CEO. Many continue to reach out to me directly as the company navigates complex technology, market, competitive, and geopolitical dynamics. NVIDIA is a once-in-a-generation company.
If the Board of Directors decides that my return is in the best interest of our shareholders, our employees, the company, and America, I would be honored to answer these calls and return as CEO.
Stock markets have fallen across Europe and in New York, ahead of Nvidia's results after today's closing Wall Street bell.
The tech-focused Nasdaq led the fallers, down 1.6%.
In London, the FTSE 100 posted its biggest one-day fall since March, falling by 1.76%.
Investors are eager to hear tonight whether Nvidia is sticking to its financial guidance, following the scandal which forced out CEO JensenHuang last week.
In a joint statement, the US Department of Justice and Department of Commerce said they had been investigating Singapore-based firm Megaspeed since 2024.
China has hit back after the US closed a loophole which allowed Chinese firms to access Nvidia-powered data centres in third-party countries.
China's foreign ministry spokesperson GuoJiakun said Beijing would take "necessary measures" to safeguard its own interests, saying:
"The US has repeatedly overstretched the concept of national security, abused export controls and even interfered in China's normal trade and technological cooperation with other countries, unjustifiably suppressing the development of China's high-tech industries."
Jensen Huang should not be reinstated as Nvidia's CEO, argues Jeffrey Sonnenfeld, the Lester Crown Professor of Leadership Practice at the Yale School of Management.
Writing in Time Magazine today, Sonnenfeld argues that Nvidia's board were wise to closed the door on Huang's return, and shouldn't let it be forced open again.
Sonnenfeld writes:
That door should stay shut. Over 33 years, Huang built the company at the center of the AI era, but in our view, his conduct nevertheless made his position untenable. He misled directors about undisclosed relationships and oversaw a firm no one could check-a breakdown in trust that was magnified in China, where he advocated loosening export controls even as restricted chips reached Chinese military units and a Shanghai facility tied to Alice Huang's network.
The political push to restore him rests on the billions his most prominent advocates have riding on his customer-financing web and on misleading geopolitical spin, at the expense of genuine shareholder concerns and national defense.
Sonnenfeld also argues that a board that can be overruled by a petition has "no function", concluding:
Nvidia's directors deferred to Huang for years and intervened late, and reversing course under outside pressure now would merely extend a habit of deference. Instead, the board should let its investigation finish, restore standalone Singapore revenue disclosures, and select a successor on the merits. Huang spent 33 years building an enterprise the AI era cannot do without. Now comes the defining test of a great company-whether it can outlast the person who built it.
Jensen Huang: I love our country, and I love Nvidia
Here's the full statement issued by JensenHuang, signalling he would like to return to his former job running Nvidia.
Over the past week, I've been overwhelmed by the love and support of friends, industry colleagues, and people I've never met. Thank you to everyone who has shown kindness to my family and me. It means the world to me.
I came to the United States 53 years ago, and becoming an American citizen is one of the greatest gifts and proudest moments of my life. NVIDIA has been my life's work. Building it into the company it is today alongside my colleagues has been a privilege and an honor. Nowhere but in America could a company like NVIDIA be possible. I love our country, and I love NVIDIA.
I did not live up to the standards expected of everyone at NVIDIA, and I have made serious mistakes in my personal life. I created problems for the Board that I deeply regret. I own my mistakes completely, and I am committed to cooperating with the Board's independent investigation.
Since my departure, I've seen an outpouring of calls from NVIDIA's employees, investors, business partners, and customers for me to return as CEO. Many continue to reach out to me directly as the company navigates complex technology, market, competitive, and geopolitical dynamics. NVIDIA is a once-in-a-generation company. If the Board of Directors decides that my return is in the best interest of our shareholders, our employees, the company, and America, I would be honored to answer these calls and return as CEO.
Thank you again to everyone who has shared their good wishes. I am profoundly humbled by your support. To my family: I love you, and I will spend the rest of my life being worthy of yours.
This is quite the intervention from JensenHuang, just five hours before Nvidia is due to release its latest financial results.
It makes it harder for the company's board to avoid questions about its succession plans, and heaps the pressuer on interim CEO ColetteKress to calm investors' nerves about the company's outlook.
Jensen Huang says he is prepared to return as Nvidia CEO
Newsflash: Former Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang has issued a statement saying he would be "honoured" to return to the role, less than a week after resigning.
In a statement issued to the media, Huang - whe quit last week over an affair with an alleged Chinese spy - says:
"I did not live up to the standards expected of everyone at NVIDIA, and I have made serious mistakes in my personal life. I created problems for the Board that I deeply regret.
Last weekend, an open letter called on Nvidia's board to reinstate Huang while an independent investigation was conducted.
Today, Huang says:
"If the Board of Directors decides that my return is in the best interest of our shareholders, our employees, the company, and America, I would be honored to answer these calls and return as CEO."
However, Nvidia's board indicated yesterday they are not considering reinstating Huang as CEO....
Jay Aldebert, chief growth officer atInternational Services,says Nvidia is confronting several crises at once:
An employee rebellion: Growing internal pressure to bring Huang back, with warnings that critical AI talent could walk away.
A leadership vacuum: Can Kress reassure investors, customers and employees while the board searches for a permanent CEO?
A Wall Street confidence test: Will strong earnings be enough to stabilize the stock, or has the leadership crisis fundamentally changed Nvidia's valuation?
Washington and China: New scrutiny of Nvidia's China-related business and national security questions adds another layer of uncertainty.
The future of AI: Could a prolonged crisis at the world's leading AI chipmaker disrupt investment, innovation and the companies dependent on Nvidia's technology?
